---
title: "Opposing criterion directions"
subtitle: "4.2 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 12 and 19"
description: "How criterion disagreement and posterior uncertainty affect the cost of ranking a pair."
---

Two criteria can favor opposite directions for the same pair. To identify those pairs, the matrix compares the
error probabilities for both directions on each criterion.

```{=html}
<div id="app" class="prx-app column-page"></div>
<script src="../../js/vendor/d3.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/vendor/plot.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/bundles/conflict-pairs.js"></script>
<script>window.__prxApp = PRX["conflict-pairs"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("app"));</script>
```

The bars give the weighted costs of stating either direction or withholding the comparison. These costs can be
similar when the criteria agree within each state but the order changes across states. They can also be similar
when the criteria disagree about a pair whose values are known. The finite examples distinguish these two
possibilities. A common grade report must also reconcile the chosen direction with its other comparisons.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Six sites, B–C.** The equal-weight costs are .4841 for B above C and .5159 for C above B. The map has 3
  opposing pairs. Withholding is cheaper for this pair on its own, but these actions do not yet form a common grade.
- **Thirty sites.** There are 397 opposing pairs. For the selected pair, the smaller expected directional cost is
  .3652. Each criterion has equal error weight; the table keeps its separate errors visible.
- **Certain opposition.** The two directions each cost .5000; withholding costs .2000. Here the smaller directional
  cost is also the statewise conflict quantity. The additional boundary preset shows every action sharing the
  minimum when withholding has the same cost.
- **Uncertain agreement.** The smaller posterior directional cost is still .5000, but statewise γ is 0 in each
  state. The criteria agree within every state; uncertainty about which state holds creates the directional cost.
- **Zero error weight.** The opposing pair stays on the map, while its cheaper direction costs 0 and the
  reverse costs 1.0000. The criterion with zero weight still favors the reverse direction, but its error adds nothing to the weighted cost.
- **Latent equality.** In **Data and exact values**, the first criterion’s two directional errors are .6000 and .9000,
  both above one half, yet it prefers the smaller one. The other criterion prefers the opposite direction. Both weighted directions cost .7500; comparing
  errors with their reverse detects this disagreement even with equality mass.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A strict direction counts as wrong when the two values are equal. Comparing the two error probabilities
therefore identifies the preferred direction even if both probabilities exceed one half. The map includes
criteria with zero weight. In each state, γ is the smaller cost of the two strict directions. Across states,
uncertainty about the true values can raise the expected cost, and the two sources need not separate uniquely.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
library(postrank)
pr_tutorial$two$e["B", "C", ]
```
:::
